speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Excellent humour because there is no election this morning.

As we were saying, Bill C-74 is a very important piece of legislation. It is important for all the reasons that my colleague at that time-he is temporarily not my colleague-Mr. Robichaud from New Brunswick. I can now say his name because he is not currently a member of this House.
A very fine member.

That will change with the next election, but my colleague at that time who led off the debate on the bill in June when we started second reading on this bill, did a very good job at that particular time.
I have to give credit to my friend for St. John's East. This is another example of how he and I, to quote a mutual friend, are cheek to cheek on so many issues.
Two peas in a pod.

He promised me this morning that he would say that my friend, Fernand Robichaud, did a good
job when he introduced for the opposition this bill at second reading. He laid out very well many of the reasons why we are in support of this good piece of legislation.
Perhaps before we go to the substance of this particular bill, we ought just to pause for a moment to reflect on what I just said. We believe this is a good piece of legislation.
So often we get flayed in this House by the government for always being against everything. The public is getting the message that we will be against it if we have reason to believe it is not good for the country. That is why we are so unalterably opposed to Bill C-21, the Unemployment Insurance Act, and why we voted against it and will do so again if the government brings it before the House again. That is why we are unalterably opposed to the goods and services tax legislation.
It is also, by the same token, why we are for the bill now before us here, Bill C-74. It addresses a number of the issues that the industry has been asking for, that fishermen have been asking for, for a long, long time. Indeed, perhaps the only question is why it has taken so long to get the legislative proposals to the stage they are today. But better late than never. At least we are now going to beef up the penalties for polluters, people who go out and dump in the ocean. We are going to see to it that if they insist on dumping harmful substances in our oceans, they are going to have to pay the price for it.
Pollution of fish habitat is unconscionable in the first instance and it can no longer be allowed to happen. There is a bunch of people, a bunch of cowards, who in the dead of night are emptying their bilge tanks and dumping crude. They are messing up the habitat there. They are messing up my front yard, in effect. Don Jamieson, one of my predecessors in this particular seat, the Burin-St. George's seat, put it so well many years ago when he was talking about the geographic confines of Burin-St. George's. He said that it must be the only electoral riding in the world which is 1,800 miles long, referring to the coast line, and a quarter of a mile wide. That is true. The only qualification I would make on Don Jamieson's statement is that it is now 2,500 miles long and a quarter of a mile wide because they have added Stephenville and the Port au Port peninsula since Don's time.
October 12, 1990

The point I make stands. It is that the people who live in Burin-St. George's, like the people who live in all but a handful of communities in Newfoundland and Labrador, live within gunshot, within view of the ocean. It is their front yard; it is their doorstep. They almost step in the water when they step out their front door. The whole history of Newfoundland, the whole history of the settlement of Newfoundland, was that people selected a spot near to the fishing ground. That was the prime parameter, the main reason that communities like Francois in my riding, like Grey River, and like Rencontre East. They were not selected for the reasons that Carleton Place down here a few miles from us was selected. I suppose one of the reasons had to do with the fact that it was on or near a good highway network. The people who settled in those communities in the 1600s and the 1700s did not know what a highway looked like. Their highway was the ocean. Their bread and butter was the ocean.
To this day in 1990 the bread and butter for the people who live in Garnish, for the people who live in McCal-lum, for the people who live in Grand Bruit is the ocean. Their highway still is first and foremost the ocean. It is true that one of those communities I just mentioned, Garnish, also happens to be hooked up to the Burin peninsula highway. That allows them to get to education facilities, to hospital facilities, and to shopping facilities; but the highway that allows them to get their bread and butter is still by and large the ocean, particularly for the fishermen who live in Garnish and other communities along that coast. It is their highway. It is their breadbasket. It is their front yard. For all those reasons we do not take a very kind view of people, of cowards in the night, who empty their bilge tanks in our front yard, who mess up our breadbasket, and who strew our highway, our ocean, with their leavings or their waste products.
I salute the minister of fisheries. I salute his parliamentary secretary, the gentleman from St. John's East. I salute those who take-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Who? Really?
Yes, I salute the gentleman from St. John's East.
Isn't he a Conservative?

Now the question comes up: "Isn't he a Conservative?" That question is asked all the time in

Newfoundland. Is he a member of the Conservative Party? The answer is yes. Is he at heart a Liberal? I will let him answer that question. I can only tell you that I have seen him sometimes when he thinks nobody is looking doing very liberal things.
Such as?

Such as bringing in this kind of legislation. Let's give the man from St. John's East credit where credit is due. I would put it the other way around. I would say to him that he is modest and all that, but I would submit to the House that the parliamentary secretary is one of the reasons why we have this piece of legislation here today.
Did you vote for him?
One of the problems with my good friend here just off to my right, philosophically and otherwise-
No, just otherwise.

One of the problems with my friend from York South-Weston, Toronto, is that sometimes he takes a particular example and generalizes. Because I happen to believe that the gentleman from St. John's West is supporting here a good piece of legislation, the kind of legislation that a Liberal government would write were it in office at the moment, that does not mean that I am going to get carried away and suggest that all the things he does needs to be embraced.
For example, he opposes the variable entrance requirement. He voted against it twice in this House.
Does he support the GST?
He supports the GST.
Shocking.

There are differences between the member for St. John's East and us, but that does not mean that we cannot pool our resources when it comes to something as important to our respective ridings as this particular bill. That is what we are doing in this particular instance.
I say to my friend from York-South Weston that when I went to university in Boston some years ago- and they had universities in those days-

Did you graduate?

That is another question. When I went to university in those days in Boston I had a professor who when using the example that was current at the time said: "All Indians walk in single file. At least the one I saw did." Of course he was making a very important point, that we ought not to overgeneralize from one particular instance.
I am just encouraged that the hon. member for St. John's East is onside on this particular bill, but I am not going to get overly excited that he is about to cross the floor to join us, because that would create a whole set of problems on its own.
The bill is a good bill because it is going to chase down those cowards in the night, those people who when nobody is looking dump their waste in my front yard, in the ocean off Newfoundland. That has got to stop, and I believe this bill goes a long way toward helping to put an end to that kind of cowardice.
If we want to get into one or two details, the very first amendment in this bill would increase the fines for general fishing violations. Quite apart from the pollution issue that I have spent a few moments on, this bill would also increase fines for general fishing violations.
At the moment offenders are liable to a $5,000 fine or a 12-month prison sentence. The new bill increases that fine to a maximum of $100,000. As my good friend and the former premier of Newfoundland would have said, "not $10,000, $20,000, $30,000 or $50,000, but $100,000 all the way up from $5,000".
I commend the drafters of the bill and the people in this House who are responsible for increasing that fine all the way from $5,000 to $100,000 in the case of a summary conviction and $500,000 on indictment, as the maximum for the indictable offence. That is exactly as it should be, and we on this side have no difficulty supporting the bill.
We come to a third point which this bill addresses. We talked so far about the question of pollution of the fish habitat. We talked about the bill's intention to bring in heftier penalties. There is another issue of course, and that is the question of adequate surveillance.
We happen to believe over here-and we have said so many times-that if the government is failing the fishermen, the fish plant workers, and the fishing industry on a
number of counts-I could go into that, but let me stick with a particular item-it is failing them most miserably in the area of surveillance or, more to the point, the lack of adequate surveillance.
I could take you, Mr. Speaker, to a community in my riding called Seal Cove in Fortune Bay. I remember one time last winter when I was there just over the Christmas season. It was seven o'clock or eight o'clock at night and it was dark. I was sitting at a kitchen table having a bit of saltfish and so on with one of my friends, and we looked out the window.
What is saltfish and so on?

He wants to know about the so on. We had saltfish. It is a good question. He wants to know what we had for supper. We had boiled saltfish, we had boiled potatoes, and we had what we call drawn butter. We had a few onions. It was a good combination.
While we were having our bit of saltfish and potatoes and drawn butter, I looked out the window into the darkness and I saw those lights. They are almost up there. I say to my host: "I thought I knew the harbour. There are no houses in that direction. What are the lights doing out there? There should only be water out there". He said: "Yes, that is all there is. That is the harbour, of course". He said: "These are not lights from a house in Seal Cove. These are lights from the foreign boats". I said: "They must be right on top of the wharf". He said: "Yes, just about".
They are supposed to be off 12 miles somewhere. They are so close that, as you look out this guy's kitchen window, you have to stare up to see the light on the mast because they are right in on the shoreline. Why are they in there? Because those foreign ships and the captains on those foreign, be they Spanish or Portuguese- in this case they happen to have been French-know that surveillance in Canada is an eight to four job. It is basically an eight to four, Monday to Friday job. You don't push your luck if you are the captain on one of those boats between those hours. After four o'clock, particularly after dark, you have a free run of it. It is the equivalent in urban terms, to use an example that maybe people in more urban centres might identify with, of saying that the cops are only going to police the streets at certain hours of the day.
October 12, 1990

Guess what happens at the other hours. Guess what the irresponsible people do. Guess what the drunken driver does. Guess what people who would breach the law do. They obviously time their actions to ensure that they are not breaking the law when the cops are policing. That is basically what is happening in another context. That is what is happening right there off Seal Cove, Fortune Bay in my example and off all those communities.
The ocean cops, the people who are supposed to be providing surveillance, I do not blame them. They have not been given the person-years, the manpower, the womanpower, or the boats and facilities to do their job. They are prepared to have additional numbers out there. It is not their problem. It is the problem of a political decision that has been taken, that in the interest of scrounging a few bucks we are going to sacrifice an entire fishery. That is what is happening out there.
In my example, off Seal Cove that night, here were French draggers within literally a thousand feet of the shore where the law said they ought to be 12 miles off.
That does not happen one night. That happens literally every night of the year during the appropriate fishing season. It happens every single night without exception.
The authorities have been told many times. They say "we know", and then throw up their hands and ask: "What can we do about it?" If they provide surveillance at night, they will have none during the day because they are locked into a very tight schedule in terms of what kinds of resources they can expend on providing surveillance.
If there is one weakness in this bill, it is that it does not do any more than pay lip service to that important question of surveillance. That is a big term for what we saw that night out of the kitchen window in Seal Cove. That is what Newfoundlanders all along that 2,500 miles of coastline in my riding see. It is what people along the coastline in the riding of the member for St. John's East see every night. They see people raping their fish stocks, and they see it being done blatantly though in the dead of night. They are allowed to do it for a very particular reason, because they know all too well that the Government of Canada does not have either the political will or

the resources, as the case may be, to get out and protect our fisheries. That is sad, but it is true.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a very difficult position because I want so much to comment on some of the things that my colleague has said, but first I want to thank him for his very kind words, and for his support in a number of areas of the fisheries.
Yes, he and I agree on some matters. He voted against the variable entrance requirement last November when we passed Bill C-21. We disagree certainly on the goods and services tax, which will create jobs in my province and his as well. But we certainly agree on things like overfishing and some of the actions that should be taken there.
I want to express in this House my appreciation for his very active, vocal and visible support in the activities and the undertakings of a number of people to draw the attention of the world to this tragic problem.
I also want to congratulate him on his clearly different approach to this piece of legislation than of his colleagues. I have been stunned by the attitude of some of his colleagues which was based on the assumption that everybody in the fishery would be subject to the provisions of the Fisheries Act because everybody in the fishery was committing an offence.
The real approach, and the approach of my friend opposite, is that this Fisheries Act with its $100,000, $500,000 and in some cases much larger fines is for those that a breaking the law. It is those who are jeopardizing the fishery and putting at risk the resource for the 99 per cent of the fishermen who obey the law, who have conservation on their minds. I appreciate his approach because it is very different from what we head the other day. I think it is an important distinction.
However, I would like to comment very briefly on the question of surveillance. I remind my friend opposite that observers will be on all foreign vessels fishing inside 200 miles. They will have new powers given to them by the Minister of Fisheries and will play much less of a monitoring role and much more of a role of imposing law. We have seen dramatically increased air surveillance out of St. John's and the other Atlantic provinces.

For about the same amount of money the number of hours have been increased to well over 3,500, which have been provided by the-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Is this debate or comment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
This is questions and comments.
I also remind him that we have new vessels in the gulf to support the surveillance opportunities.
My colleague made a very good speech, a very flattering speech for the government. I thank him for all he has done. I think he is right in recognizing that surveillance is absolutely critical. I just want to remind him that we have moved very quickly and very dramatically over the last 18 months to address exactly that question.

Mr. Speaker, my friend mentioned the GST in passing. If he genuinely believes that the GST is going to create jobs in Newfoundland, he must be making an announcement that the centre that was going to Summerside is going to Newfoundland because the only jobs that are going to be created by the GST are those jobs done in Summerside and an appalling lot here in Ottawa, appalling lot in terms of numbers, not the quality of the people hired, mind you-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Don't be so sure.

So outside of Ottawa, unless he is moving the capital to Newfoundland, which is not a bad idea, unless he is moving the tax centre from Summer-side to Newfoundland which is not a bad idea in Newfoundland terms but a lousy idea in Summerside terms, unless one or two of the above, then I would say that he is not being very candid on this issue.
Let us come to the issue of surveillance. The member says that there are going to be observers on all the boats within the 200 mile limit. Is he telling us that the government is now reneging or otherwise abrogating the treaty, the last agreement between Canada and France?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: I note what you are saying.

Exactly. Because, Mr. Speaker, in the last 24 months his other cheek-to-cheek friend, the member for St. John's West, went out and signed one of the more crazy documents ever. Basically the agreement with France says, "From now on if you want to rape our fish stock you have got to give us notice." That is what the document said. France may say it differently, Mr. Speaker. Under the agreement, signed in 1988 I believe, Canada has to say to France, "We want to board your ship. We want to board this particular ship." We, Canada, have agreed in writing to give notice that the day we come to check on them we are going to give them lead time so they can get ready.
Well, let's think that one through. What do you think will happen if we say to France next week that we are going to put an observer on its boat? Do you think France will be stunned enough, stupid enough, on that particular trip to commit any violations? That is what we have locked ourselves into with respect to the Canada-France agreement of 1988.
If the member for St. John's West tells the House that we are going to have observers on all the foreign boats within the 200-mile limit, I say to him that, in principle, it is a great idea but he is wrong at least in one important respect that comes to mind without having benefit of checking my notes. I can tell him right off the top of my head that he is wrong in so far as the Canada-France agreement is concerned because under that agreement, as he well knows, we have to give prior notice to the French that we want to put an observer on board the boat.
That is like saying to me, "Simmons, drive down the highway at 150 miles an hour for 10 miles, but after 10 miles there are cops." Now what do you think I am going to do when I get to the 150-mile mark? That is exactly what the French fishermen are doing. They have been given notice in the agreement. They have it in writing that they will be given notice if they are going to be raided. Well, if I were them I would be on my best behaviour during the raid.
The member and I agree that we have observers on the vessels by prior arrangement. They know in all cases before the fact that there are going to be observers aboard. But more to the point-here's the point that I think my friend from St. John's East misses; I will say it in a sentence and then I will sit down-it is not important to know which boats the observers are on. If you are out to break the law it is more important to know which ones they are not on. They also know that, too.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
The member for Burin-St. George's has given a very good speech with regard to Bill C-74 and it shows beyond a shadow of doubt that the expertise with regard

to fisheries related matters is certainly on this side of the House.
I wonder if he would care to comment with regard to other issues of surveillance. It is fine to have provisions under the act in order to increase the various penalties and sanctions. Could the hon. member indicate to the House whether or not, as a result of Bill C-74, additional individuals will be retained by the Government of Canada in order to facilitate the enforcement of those new laws. It is my understanding and that of some other colleagues that the Government of Canada is not intending to proceed with the hiring of additional individuals in order to assist with the enforcement of these new standards.

I thank my friend for Cape Breton-East Richmond. This is my first opportunity to congratulate him publicly on his latest achievement, having been designated by our leader, Jean Chretien, the next member for Beausejour, as the chief Whip of the Liberal Party. I want to congratulate my friend.
Mr. Speaker, I see your signal that I am out of time so I will be very quick and to the point. He asked a question and then he answers it. Are there going to be additional enforcement personnel? Of course he answered the question because it is blatantly obvious to the whole world that this government is going to bring in some marvellous legislation, legislation that we can support. But it is a case again that this government does not put its money where its mouth is. It says fine words, and nobody can knock this piece of legislation.
What it can knock and what it does knock, and what the gentleman for Cape Breton-East Richmond just knocked in effect, is the appalling fact that this government is going to create the mandate for extra surveillance and then fail to provide the resources, the manpower, the womanpower, the person-years to follow up to enforce that surveillance. That is the tragedy.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to participate in this debate on Bill C-74, amendments to the Fisheries Act. I want to join with colleagues on this side in giving just due to the
Government Orders
Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who I know has some understanding.
Don't get carried away.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I am being very liberal, Mr. Speaker, when I say some understanding of some of the concerns of individuals in Atlantic Canada.
The substance of this bill, has received the support of many of my colleagues on this side. I know that the parliamentary secretary has had a fair amount to do in making certain that this bill has come forward.
I want to put on the record, though, that by increasing summary conviction fines up to $100,000 for general fisheries offences, and then indictable offences up to $500,000 with options for imprisonment of one or two years, I can concur with that. I fully understand, as my colleague has said, the importance of increasing those fines.
There is another part to the equation. It is well and good to have sanctions under a statute, but if those sanctions cannot be enforced by the Crown, it is all for nought. Members can argue, and argue correctly, that this is a signal to those who wish to breach the Fisheries Act that there will be substantial fines against them.
On the other side of the coin, there is no reasonable guarantee that fisheries officers and the Crown will supply the individuals to do the enforcing. Therefore, one has to question the bill both from an intellectual perspective as well as from a practical perspective. It is great to have a sanction, but if one cannot enforce that sanction, it is just window dressing.
There are fines of up to $300,000 on summary conviction for the alteration of fish habitat. On an indictment, it is $1 million. The Crown in a criminal case has the option to proceed on summary conviction or it has the option to proceed on indictable offence, depending upon the value of the product which is in question.
I have great confidence in our judiciary system, but what the act fails to state is what is a minimum fine. I know members opposite and perhaps members on this side would agree that the judiciary has to have some latitude in the exercising of its role in the adjudication of different cases. But there is a big difference on summary conviction when you talk of a hundred bucks versus $300,000. A substantial difference.

October 12, 1990
Government Orders
Likewise, if you proceed under the indictable, there is quite a difference between $301,000 and $1 million. I would have thought that somewhere within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, and to use a phrase-aided and abetted-by the Department of Justice, the bureaucracy in the minister's office would have wanted to tty to clarify for us what the minimum fine is going to be. I am afraid that some of these fines will not have a minimum, but in fact will end up being very, very, low, thereby defeating the purpose or the purposes of the act.
Again, where are the practical aspects of the act? Have we heard from ministers of the Crown that additional individuals will be retained? Have we heard that various enforcement agencies are going to be utilized to enforce these sanctions? We have not heard that. We have heard the opposite. In point of fact, no additional individuals will be retained in order to enforce the sanctions under that particular statute.
The same sanctions under Bill C-74 have to do with the pollution of fish habitat. The Harris report, the Hache report, and, I believe, under the auspices of the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program, all alluded to greater sanctions under the Fisheries Act, and I think the parliamentary secretary, who is nodding his head, would concur with me on that.
There is a bit of a concern, and I just flag it. I do not think it is an overwhelming omission, but I think it has to be put on the record, and it is this. Is this new law and these new sanctions, under the Fisheries Act, discriminatory in this sense? Many individuals, in the Atlantic fisheries particularly, believe the sanctions are earmarked for the inshore fishermen.
I hope the parliamentary secretary would avail himself, when it is his turn to speak, to inform the House in greater detail. But there is that concern. These sanctions are in place and, if they are to be enforced, they will be enforced on one sector of our fishery, namely, the inshore fishery.
The policies opposite and the made-in-Canada recession, or as the Prime Minister says, the slowdown or the shutdown-whichever one you wish to pick-have had an overwhelmingly negative impact on inshore fishermen in Atlantic Canada. Members on this side, my colleagues, the hon. members for Cardigan and Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, have brought to the attention of the House on several occasions our attempts to provide a variable entrance rate, to assist fishermen. But
the government, for whatever reason, refuses to put that into play in order to assist our fishermen and our inshore fishermen, in particular.
There is legitimate concern out there because of the recession and because fishermen are not obtaining the benefits of the variable entrance rate which was in place for 14 years. It was brought in annually by the respective governments opposite as well as this party. The governing party does not wish to go along with that at the present time. And, of course, there is the fact of fish stocks. All of those, collectively, have played very negatively on our inshore fishermen and now the sanctions of Bill C-74 seem to suggest that it is discriminatory against the inshore fishermen.
Why would I say that on the floor of the House. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because there are some groups who have not had meaningful consultations or who feel that the consultations that they did have have not been meaningful. In particular, they have been organizations in the inshore fishery.
I would hope that when the bill is referred to a legislative committee that it will make a concerted effort to seek out those groups who have expressed legitimate concern about the discriminatory aspects of Bill C-74 and, as they say, clear the air by having that rectified.
The industry has generally supported the provisions of Bill C-74. But I want to flip from the inshore to the offshore. I hope the parliamentary secretary, when he gets up to speak later, will be able to outline in spades for members of the House as to what the Government of Canada is going to do to enforce the sanctions under Bill C-74 with regard to the corporate sector.

We are very supportive of businesses and free enterprise, but there has to be a measure of fairness. Under the provisions of Bill C-74, are we going to charge an inshore fisherman $250,000 because he has a general offence against the Fisheries Act? Then National Sea Products, bailed out by banks and governments, will get a fine of $150. That is the fairness, but there is no minimum. There is wide latitude, and we know what happens. We have clear evidence before us. We see it all the time where inshore fishermen are sustaining the worst, while in other instances individuals do not share their fair burden. I

There are several other points I want to raise because I think they are germane to the debate. I made that argument with regard to fisheries, and now I am making it with regard to the environment. Either one is serious or one is not serious. Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the TVeasury
Board): Mr. Speaker, in the case we are talking about today, the government's position is that we want a complete environmental assessment of the project. Mr. Speaker, this week has shown clearly that the finance minister has lost the confidence of the country. Major business groups attached his policies yesterday. Important think tanks say he is wrong. Provinces representing over half the population of this country are taking him to court to try to stop the GST.
I ask the finance minister what his government is going to do to change its policies to win some confidence from people and to stop this economic decline.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the hon. member has drawn that conclusion. It says here clearly: "Mr. Thibault says our message is not directed only to Mr. Wilson. It is a problem we have as a country on a federal, local and provincial level. We are not just talking here about the federal government or the provincial government. We are talking about Canada and the Canadian people."
October 12, 1990

What these people are pointing out is that we have a national problem. It needs a national response.
They have gone on to say: "Mr. Wilson's performance in the area of government spending has been better than all of the provinces."
We have a major problem and the rhetoric which the hon. member uses is not helpful in dealing with the problem. What would be helpful from the hon. member is how he feels we could get the deficit down, as is the objective of these business leaders, as was the objective of the Economic Council of Canada, as was the objective of most knowledgeable and intelligent observers of the political scene.

Mr. Speaker, let me suggest that the minister is very selectively quoting from business leaders who yesterday said things such as "bankruptcies among small and mid-size companies are soaring. Business confidence has dropped to levels not seen since the 1981-82 recession".
They talked about "the damage caused by Canada's dismal fiscal policy". I want to ask the finance minister about this. He has described this slowdown as a healthy thing for the economy. Is that his only answer to the thousands of people who are being thrown out of work across this country? Is that his only answer to governments that are facing vastly increased deficits at the provincial level? Is that his only answer or is his answer cartoons in newspapers to try to prop up the GST?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should reflect back to the number of statements I have made in this House on many occasions over the last six years as Minister of Finance. I have taken great pleasure in seeing business activity strong, people having good jobs and taking advantage of the opportunities that are there.
I recognized some two years ago that we had a problem that was derived directly from the inflationary pressures that were in the economy and if we did not get those inflationary pressures under control, we were going to get back to the type of recession we had in 1981-82. I would like to avoid that.
Oral Questions
I want to do everything I can to ensure that we get on a path of non-inflationary strong growth in the future. That requires us to go through this temporary period where we have a slowdown in the economy, so that we can get those inflationary pressures under control. As we get the inflationary pressures under control, we will be able to get interest rates down. The benefits of that will seep into every nook and cranny of the economy. That is the best thing we can do to get the economy moving again.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
I am speaking on behalf of thousands of Canadians who got their walking papers this week, in particular the 550 employees who were told last month that they were surplus to operational requirements of the Tridon Corporation in Burlington.
The minister will know that at the same time he is leading Canadian workers in a made-in-Canada recession, he is permitting the export of taxpayer-financed technology to the United States.
I would like to ask the minister a veiy specific question. Given that it was government financing that permitted the development of two new products that are going to be creating thousands of jobs in a cheaper labour market in the southern United States right now, is he prepared today to order his colleague, the Minister for Industry, Science and Technology, to put a lien on all Canadian technology and all equipment at the Tridon plant in Canada so that they cannot spirit more Canadian jobs south as a result of his fiscal, monetary and trade policies?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance and it is very simple. Many individuals and families in northern Canada order their basic groceries directly from southern Canadian suppliers. These groceries are shipped to them by air or by sealift and, of course, there are freight charges.
Will these northern families have to pay the goods and services tax on the freight cost of their groceries?

Mr. Speaker, there is no goods and services tax on the freight cost. That is credited out of the cost of all food in any part of the country. That is particularly important to people in northern Canada. There will be no goods and services tax in the price of food after January 1, 1991, whereas today, there is federal sales tax on the transportation costs and also on other costs of food that we consume. It amounts to some one to two percentage points.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Northerners will be better off.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Of course, businesses get tax credits on the freight, but individuals do not.
I have a letter in my hand from a major Canadian air carrier that states: "The vast majority of shipments destined to northern communities usually contain a mix of various commodities, that would make it quite difficult for our front-line staff to manage should a tax waiver be implemented for specific types of cargo". They have not been instructed by the government to exempt food shipments from the goods and services tax, nor do they have the staff to isolate taxable and non-taxable commodities.
Will the minister now admit that certain Canadians, namely northern Canadians, will be taxed on their food?

Mr. Speaker, I would be interested in receiving the information that the hon. member has read out. It sounds to me from what is said in the document that he read from that there is a misunderstanding on how the tax on the food today will be changed as a result of the GST.
October 12, 1990

The simple fact is that all federal sales tax today, whether it is on transportation, packaging, computers, cash registers, or building materials to build stores, will be backed out of the system so that under the GST there will be no tax on the cost of food. As I indicated in my earlier response, that amounts to some one to two percentage points of the cost of food. This will ensure that all food that is consumed by northerners will be removed from tax and will be cheaper.

The minister has said to the media, and in a letter to the Canadian Medical Association, that she would not proclaim the bill unless the doctors were ready. The doctors are not ready.
Will the minister keep her promise to the doctors of Canada, to the women of Canada, and will she guarantee today in the House not to proclaim this regressive, criminal legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been working very closely with the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada to deal with the concerns that its members have expressed. I am very hopeful that that consultation will be successful in alleviating many of the doctors' concerns.
In my discussions, both with the executive of the organization and with doctors across the country-and my consultations are ongoing-I find that their concerns are based on a misunderstanding of the legislation. It is a labour-intensive process to try to get that message across and to explain how the bill works. There is a lot of misunderstanding. As I have said before, doctors are not lawyers. I have committed myself to doing that because I think it is very, very important for the doctors' well being and for the well being of the women of Canada. I will
Oral Questions
keep to my commitment that the bill will not be proclaimed until that process is complete.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that what the minister means is that she will not proclaim the bill as long as doctors are in opposition to the bill. The minister has been very patronizing, thinking that she can explain the bill to doctors and to women and that they will agree that there is not a devastating effect on access for women.
Tomorrow thousands of women will be on the streets of Canada demonstrating against this bill. Will the Minister commit herself to ensure these women and doctors that the bill will not be proclaimed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing that I say about the implications of Bill C-43 that is not supported by independent experts in criminal law. I certainly accept the right of people to protest on either side of the abortion issue, as they will do tomorrow, and as it happens every day on the other side of the issue outside this building.
I would like to caution the hon. member that, in the process of people arguing their political views on this particular issue, a distortion of the implications of Bill C-43 is not, in my view, a legitimate tactic. Much of the misinformation that doctors have about Bill C-43 and how it works does not come from the Department of Justice, does not come from the Government of Canada, and does not come from people who understand it. It comes from irresponsible statements made by people in pursuing their particular policy goals.
I would like to see from the hon. member a commitment to fight the battle on fair grounds, not to distort Bill C-43, and not to create fears that are unfounded. Doctors have nothing to fear from this legislation. To create these kinds of fears is to play very high stakes politics, which I think is unconscionable for anyone on this sensitive issue.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Valcourt that Bill C-74, an act to amend the Fisheries Act and to amend the Criminal Code in consequence thereof be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate on amendments to the Fisheries Act, Bill C-74, and to join my colleagues from Burin-St. George's and Cape Breton-East Richmond in supporting the broad thrust of this legislation, which is to increase the fines and penalties for violations of the Fisheries Act and related offences.
In addition, we also have mentioned that we have certain reservations concerning the bill and with the policies of the government. Amendments need to be put in place to accompany the bill and I will speak to those a little later. Before I do, I would like to begin with a digression.
It would be remiss of me as the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, a riding that experienced in December of last year the loss of one of its major fish plants. I initiated an emergency debate to address the serious crisis in the Atlantic fishery which was manifested no less dramatically than by the situation facing the people of the town of Canso when their fish plant closed. I wish to acknowledge favourably the work that
has been done over the summer by the minister of fisheries and by the department of fisheries in seeking a solution to that very difficult situation facing the people of Canso and the people of Burgeo who are part of the solution worked out by the minister of fisheries in conjunction with participants from industry.
The plan known as the Seafreez deal which creates this new corporation operating out of Burgeo and Canso will involve a rather complicated arrangement of bartering and exchange of fish between Canada and the Soviet Union. The transfer of quota is a complicated and controversial arrangement and there has been some concern within the industry about various aspects of this deal.
I realize that the jury is still out as to whether or not the minister violated certain customary practices in arriving at this arrangement, and also whether or not he consulted widely enough before putting the deal together. We do not know whether in fact the arrangement is going to work. I certainly hope it does.
The promise has been made to secure the employment of some 500 plant workers in Canso for the indefinite future. It is essential that these be year-round jobs to ensure that the trawler fleet of Canso and Burgeo continues to fish. I cannot be blind to that effort and certainly want to support and encourage the successful resolution of that arrangement if it produces the promised results, which I hope it does.
This is an opportunity for me to say in this House that I am certainly supportive of the Seafreez deal, to the extent that it produces employment in a community that is vitally dependent on this industry. I will be participating in and evaluating very closely the broader policy aspects which are associated with the putting together of this deal. I am very familiar with the controversy that surrounds it and expect that the minister of fisheries will be sensitive to the broader industry implications of this deal. However, we will be able to debate that at some further point.
That is by means of a digression but I believe an important one, since I happen to represent the community of Canso which has been such a symbol of the crisis facing the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada over the last year.
October 12, 1990

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I will now return to the debate. As I said earlier, Bill C-74 stiffens the fines to fishing companies, fishermen, and other persons who violate various aspects of the Fisheries Act. It provides for a dramatic increase in fines for general fisheries offences, for overfishing, for discarding of fish at sea, for obstructing fisheries officers in the performance of their duties and for harassing them when they are trying to administer the Fisheries Act, and for other offences that are fisheries related.
We in the Liberal Party cannot but support those fines. The fines that were already in place in the Fisheries Act were laughable. They were no deterrents at all, particularly to the large companies that were really able to pay those fines, as the minister has said, as a cost of doing business. So clearly, the increase in fines was drastically overdue. I guess our main objection to this bill and to the measures which are in it is why has it not been introduced earlier?
We have other problems with the legislation. First of all, as was mentioned very eloquently by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond this morning, there is more to administering and to enforcing the Fisheries Act and preventing overfishing and pollution in our coastal waters than simply increasing the level of fines that fishing vessels, companies, and other interests, must pay. We have to increase the policing and surveillance of our coastal waters to ensure that those fines can actually be levied.
Unfortunately this has just not accompanied the legislation to a sufficient degree to enable, we believe, those much more realistic penalties to be enforced. And that is essential, if we are going to get under control the kinds of overfishing and discarding at sea which we have heard about over the last years. We have discussed this deepening fishing crisis and it has been reported to us through various task forces as being one of the fundamental problems underlying a severe resource crisis in many parts of Atlantic Canada today.
Mr. Speaker, we can increase the levels of fines, we can increase the protection provided fisheries officers but we have to put into place measures to increase surveillance, enforcement, and policing, so that the penalties will actually stick and so that they will actually be a deterrent to those who would commit fisheries
Government Orders
violations. That is the first point, and it has been made by others. I want to add to it by emphasizing that concern.
The other aspect of this legislation which I do not think has been mentioned, at least in the debate on second reading that I have read so far, is with respect to the particular concerns associated with the violations of fish habitat, pollution and destruction of the fish habitat.
The fines that have been imposed in this legislation for violations of fish habitat, and I will quote here from the information package which accompanies the bill, involve raising the fines from initially $5,000 on summary conviction to $300,000 on summary conviction, and from $10,000 for second and subsequent offences, to up to $1 million on indictment. There are court options of up to six months imprisonment or up to three years on indictment.
The same goes for pollution of fisheries habitat, the deposit of deleterious substances by individuals who pollute the fisheries habitat. Again, those fines have been dramatically increased. That, again, is overdue and very much necessary.
However, when the minister was describing this particular aspect of violations he was focusing on the problem of individuals or private companies for example who, in the process of building a bridge over a river or a brook, pollute that river or brook or the harbour near there. Another example would be the companies which build a facility close to a coastline or a river, thereby polluting that body of water and, in the process, destroying the fish resource. That practice has to be stopped. It requires stringent legislation to prevent that from occurring and also it should be backed up by strong enforcement mechanisms. It is also consistent with the new concern that we have for the environment, in particular our coastal waters and coastal environment.
However, there is something missing in this particular aspect of fisheries habitat control and management. It is the point that I would like to bring to this debate on Bill C-74. The Minister of Fisheries, when speaking on second reading in June, referred to the government's Green Plan proposals and told the House that this legislation fitted into the government's proposals with respect to the environment. He said it was a way of strengthening such laws as the coastal waters protection and the environmental protection legislation and a way

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

of increasing the enforcement of our environmental legislation and I agree that that needs to be done.
However, there are other aspects of the pollution of fisheries habitat which have been ignored in this legislation and I suggest are not readily dealt with by simply increasing the fines to polluters. I refer to a problem which is in my constituency and a problem which has lasted for a long time.
In the Bras d'Or Lakes in Cape Breton, which is in my constituency, we have an oyster resource located near the community of Whycocomagh. For many years, Why-cocomagh has not had a proper sewer and water system. It has not had the wherewithal to finance that sewer and water system because of the lack of a municipal tax base.
The persistent neglect of providing a mechanism for that community to install a sewer and water system, which would control and treat the sewage that now ends up in the Bras d'Or Lakes and in the bay near Whycocomagh, results in the contamination of the oyster population. Essentially, a local industry that could have employed many people in the surrounding areas at least for part of the year has been destroyed. That industry, in effect, has been decimated around the community of Whycocomagh. It has been one of the casualties of the lack of action, despite repeated requests by myself and others, to assist and support the creation of a municipal sewer and water system in that community.
There are other areas in my own constituency such as coastal waters, small harbours, and river mounts where communities are still polluting those enclosed bodies of water and adding to a pollution problem which they are powerless to control. They would not be able to stop what they are doing if they were fined $1 million or $500,000, short of packing up and leaving the community. That solution requires support and not punishment by the government.
In the months ahead the government is going to be introducing measures and legislation to deal with various problems concerning the environment. I suggest that support for municipal infrastructure is one area in which assistance by the federal government is urgently needed for environmental reasons and for the reasons I have just
mentioned. It is something that we in the Liberal Party have advocated for several years and we continue to advocate. We hope the government will see fit to adopt that as a way of dealing with one source of coastal pollution which is not readily addressed by simply imposing stricter fines, notwithstanding the fact that stricter fines are essential given the nominal levels of penalties which had existed in the Fisheries Act before.
I wanted to make that point related to the legislation. I admit that it will not necessarily find its way directly into the Fisheries Act. but the government should not pat itself on the back by saying: "Look, we have increased the fines for people polluting our coastal waters and we have increased the fines for people spoiling our fish habitat. We have done our job." It has not done its job. That is only one part of the solution.
Another part of the solution is to provide support so that municipal governments and local communities can have the wherewithal to clean up their own back yards. This will allow commercial and recreational fishermen to have a resource to exploit that has not been allowed to be contaminated by years of pollution and untreated sewage. That is only one dimension of that particular problem. I submit that it is a serious one. It is one that should not be overlooked. I believe it is related to the measures that are in the Fisheries Act amendments. It is a subject that needs to be given more serious weight by the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I probably will focus more on comments than on questions.
I want to address a couple of things that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond mentioned earlier and was not given an opportunity to respond to, despite his great admonitions that I should.
First, I refer to what my friend from Cape Breton- Highlands-Canso has said. The moving ahead of this legislation has come after considerable consultation with a great number of groups. I will just mention a few groups that DFO officials talked to: all provinces and territories, as well as a variety of advisory groups to the minister, including ARC, PARC and the Atlantic Council of Fisheries Ministers, in particular. They have supported that.
October 12, 1990

This legislation is being brought forward because of the determination of the current Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and of his predecessor, both of whom feel very strongly that one of the important ways to address some of the inequities, not only in the legislation, but in the application of the law, is to impose higher fines and to bring in new sources of information.
Both of my colleagues has asked: What is the point of having new legislation if it cannot be enforced? Under the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program, there has been $52 million over five years in addition provided for surveillance and enforcement. Offshore patrols have been increased. Inshore patrols across the Atlantic will be increased. There will be more intensive use of DFO vessels for patrolling and enforcing the law. There is more money for increased armed boarding, a practice that I do not particularly like but sometimes is necessary, and increased funds for prosecution. Of course, I need not mention the agreement that we reached with the Americans that will hopefully ensure that people cannot come and go across borders unprotected.
Another thing that has been protected is the fact that there is no minimum fine. My colleague across the way referred to the level of fines. First, I should point out that the level of penalty is consistent. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the Hazardous Products Act, the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, the National Parks Act, the Railway Safety Act and the Canadian Agricultural Products Act all have no minimum fine. It allows leeway for the courts.
Do not forget, with triple, and in some cases five times, the amount of fine, a clear message is being sent to the judiciary that we are very serious and the the judiciary is forced to respond to that.
In terms of inshore versus offshore, very clearly this act allows penalties to be applied in all ways. There is a perception, and I understand it, that we are applying it purely to the inshore. I should point out, though, that as we increase the observer coverage on the offshore vessels, as we work more and more to avoid discards, culling and highgrading, we will see more and more charges laid in the offshore than ever in the inshore.
Government Orders
Then, the question comes: How is there corporate accountability and responsibility? This act ensures that it is not just the person aboard ship who ends up in court. Licence holders can be held liable for offences. Under the new act, officers and directors of corporations can be held accountable, which is a substantial change and an important change.
There is more to come, but I wanted to take this opportunity to comment on the remarks of both my friends from Cape Breton. I appreciate their support. Sometimes I wonder if that support is consistently there. One member says that the opposition is all for it and that it is gung ho, and another seems to be a little less sure. I hope we can depend on the support of the Liberal Party of Canada for this legislation at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I say to my friend across the way that he can always depend on our support of legislation which we say we will support, just as he can always depend on our opposition to legislation which we oppose, sometimes quite vigorously.
To clarify what we said earlier, I might say that our support for this legislation is qualified. We, of course, advocate higher fines, stiffer penalties for fisheries violations. We have said that they have been long overdue. We are concerned that the means of enforcing those stiffer fines are not in place. We will be looking to see if the government is really committed to prosecuting and enforcing the higher fines and penalties that it has put in place.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank and congratulate my colleague for Cape Breton Highlands- Canso. It is certainly obvious that he understands the problem in the fishing industry.
I think my problem with Bill C-74 is what it does not contain. We have problems in Gaspereaux, Georgetown and Savage Harbour. For example, in Savage Harbour we needed a small amount of funding for the black wall or the breakwater in that area and the funding did not come. It has now been two years. With ice and a couple of winters, it is just about destroyed. If we do not get

Government Orders
some funding for things like this, the sand will move in and we will need more dredging. Of course, dredging again is a major problem. Dredging needs to be on an ongoing basis. The bill just does not seem to answer the questions for the fishermen in the Cardigan riding.
With regard to lobster, which is one of our main fisheries, fishermen are asked to go out and fish for $1.25 a pound. Well, for a delicacy, it is impossible to survive at $1.25 a pound. The problem that we have is that Bill C-74 does not address the problems for our fishery in Cardigan and Prince Edward Island.
I would like to ask my hon. colleague how he feels the barter and the catches affect plant closures, and were the catches fairly allotted to the plants?

thank my hon. colleague for his question. I agree with him that there is much that has been excluded from this piece of legislation. We will be looking from the government for constructive action on small craft harbour improvements. He listed some needed improvements in his area. I have similar improvements that are required in my area as well, including dredging, breakwater and wharf repairs.
As far as the bartering of fish, this is a very complex area in which I would not want to get into with the small amount of time that is available.
With respect to the Seafreez deal, there are a lot of questions which need to be asked from a policy point of view as to the legitimacy of the actions of the government. It will have to be looked at over a period of time as to what are the underlying principles of bartering of fish and probably setting up some rules that are agreeable to everybody about whether or not this practice-whatever it is, because we are not sure exactly what is taking place-can be regulated or allowed to continue in a fair and equitable manner.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me an honour and a pleasure to speak today on Bill C-74. First of all, I was listening to my colleague for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso and some of the questions and comments that were made at the end of his speech. I was also listening to the comments made by the member for St. John's East. He was sort of questioning whether the Liberal Party would be supporting Bill C-74.
I say to the hon. member that the Liberal Party has always had a habit of supporting bills that are good for Canadians in general, but more so for the common person, such as fishermen. Bill C-74 has my support and will have my support when it comes time for the vote. It does not solve all the problems in the fishery. We know, and you know, Mr. Speaker, that over the last year or so the fisheries have been in a state of crisis. The right hon. Prime Minister did not seem to realize that at one point in time. I think he has come back to reality and has finally realized that there are problems in the fisheries, not only in Atlantic Canada but also on the west coast. I was very surprised that we did not hear any mention today from our colleagues who sit a little farther down from me, but there are problems on the west coast as well, and some very serious problems. I was hoping to hear from them as well.
We know there are problems in Atlantic Canada. We have heard the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso many times in this House try to point out some of the problems that exist in Atlantic Canada. Let me tell you that he is doing a wonderful job for his riding and deserves a lot of credit.
The reason we support Bill C-74 in general is that it increases the penalties and fines for persons who break the Fisheries Act. I should clarify the position of our party, and I am sure the position of everyone in this House. Hon. members here feel that fishermen are basically honest and hard working individuals. There are a few out there with whom there are problems. No doubt about it. Some are foreigners. Some of them are our own. But there are a few, a very few. I would have to say 99.9 per cent of fishermen are honest, hard working people who are there to try and have gainful employment, to support their families, to support ultimately their country. Not being on the social assistance payroll is a benefit in itself to our country.
The bill tabled on June 6,1990, will bring about higher fines and penalties through the Fisheries Act. There will be higher fines and penalties for general offences, up to $100,000 on summary conviction and up to $500,000 on indictment. That same type of penalty will be for the obstruction of fisheries officers. We know that has been a problem previously.
We will also see increased fines and penalties in relation to the pollution of fish habitat. We know that has been a problem, not only the throwing overboard of
October 12, 1990

excess fish or dying fish, but oil leakage and things of that nature. That will also be included in the act. That is one of the reasons why we support such an act. It will penalize those who are not responsible enough to see what their actions are doing to the fisheries environment. It will also provide penalties and fines to anyone who fails to provide habitat information. It will require fishermen and processors to keep more detailed records.
This is an area where the bill could be improved. It might be a little difficult at this stage to judge the effect of this part of it on fishermen. It may become a little more complicated and a little too bureaucratic. Maybe that is something that should be looked at by the government.
I am glad to see that the government has looked at the Harris report and the Hache report. I am glad to see that those reports, in their wisdom, also suggested increased penalties and fines. In this case, we are glad to see that the government is listening, once and for all, to certain recommendations that will help the fisheries. We are very pleased with that.
No doubt, as an opposition member, there are always a few things that we are not pleased with. We always say the government does not go far enough. We feel that there are not enough resources put in to enforcing these new regulations and fines. I have some doubts as to how we are going to handle the Americans. I know there is a new agreement and it looks promising, but if we look at past actions of our government and foreigners fishing in what we claim to be our waters, we see that we tend to be very tough on foreign vessels, as long as they do not come from the United States. I am sure the government will treat all of these foreigners who are overfishing or breaking some of these regulations adequately and in the same way.
Also, it should be pointed out that many of the provisions and resources are going toward the inshore sector. I think there should be more effort put in the offshore sector as well. I am sure the government is aware of that. I am sure the government realizes it has problems financially. It has a major problem. It has created a Canadian recession, so to speak. We have seen examples of that this week by the experts. It is going to have to get its act together on its economic plan as soon as possible. Once that is in place, hopefully it will see fit
Government Orders
to provide more resources to the offshore sector as well and add to the inshore.
The hon. member for St. John's East mentioned the consultations that took place in the fishing industry. I am led to believe that there was not as much consultation with fishermen's associations. Yes, other groups were consulted, and I know some of the fishing associations were, but maybe there should be more consultation in regard to the final form of the legislation. I know it is not always possible, but I think it is important that the fishermen feel that this is their bill as well as the government's and that it will help the fishing industry.
Another aspect of the bill that should be questioned is the bookkeeping. I mentioned that earlier. Are we going to force fishermen to become bookkeepers and are we going to force fishermen to hire other people? As we know, with the situation as it exists in the fishing industry, a lot of them are family operations and it is very difficult for them to keep that type of information in some cases.
It was mentioned earlier that one of the other major problems, and I think it is a problem with Bill C-74, is what the bill does not contain. We have many problems in the fishing industry. One of them is a problem that is going to be addressed with this bill, we hope. We hope it will solve that problem, but there are other problems. The concern of many fishermen at this time is the absence of the government introducing a variable entrance requirement bill. I know when I mention this people get a little upset and some people who are very partisan tend to blame the Senate for holding back Bill C-21.
Yes, Bill C-21 is still in the Senate being analysed. Since 1977, the governments of the day, Conservative and Liberal, introduced a short bill every year for variable entrance requirements and it passed very quickly. That is what should have been done while Bill C-21 was being studied in the Senate, to prevent damage to workers who are unemployed, especially fishermen at this stage of the game. We know that the fishing industry has been hurt quite severely.
In defence of the Senate, I must say that- [Translation]
To give credit where credit is due, Mr. Speaker, the senators tried to remedy this situation and restore the variable entrance requirement when they sent Bill S-12 to the House of Commons on December 19, 1989. This year in June, Liberal members in this House tried once again to deal with the problems facing Canadian workers by tabling a motion from the Senate and the House of

October 12, 1990
Government Orders
Commons that would restore the variable entrance requirement. The motion was rejected by the government.

As I was saying, we tried to introduce those motions to lower the entrance requirements, especially in the rural areas. In my area of Restigouche-Chaleur the unemployment rate hovers around 17 per cent. The entrance requirements for unemployment insurance are now at 14 per cent, the same as Toronto, Vancouver, and all over Canada. If the Conservative government had passed the variable entrance requirement law as every other government had done since 1977, the variable entrance requirement to get unemployment insurance in my riding would have been at 10 per cent. It is not necessarily the senators' fault, because every other government has passed that.
There are other problems. This government has many problems. When we look at the government's monetary policy, we find that it has affected the fishing communities in Atlantic Canada and not only the fishing communities because the fishing communities have a spin-off effect. They supply the rest of the economy. The city of Halifax has concern about the fishing problems as well, because where do fishermen buy their supplies, where do they go shopping? Obviously that is going to have an effect.
I spoke the other day about the monetary policy of this government. I talked about the high interest rates, the high dollar, the cuts in regional development, the GST and the effect it will have on Atlantic Canada and on rural Canada. Actually the economy is in a mess. This government has lost credibility because this was the government that was supposed to solve the economic problems of Canada. As we have seen this week, many associations, many groups, and economic think-tanks have suggested that it is out of control. We know who to blame for that.
In conclusion, I would like to come back to the bill at hand. I am sorry that I digressed a bit, but I could not help it. We have to get a little partisan now and then. I could not help it. To come back to the bill at hand, Bill C-74, I must say that the government is moving in the right direction. It remains to be seen, though, whether
this is the right solution for the problem. We do not know whether it is going to work. We will see if there are enough resources committed to enforce the regulations. I hope there are.
The hon. member for St. John's East seems to imply that there will be resources there. I am glad to hear that. I would like to say that we are moving in the right direction and hopefully some of these problems will be solved in the very near future.
I am very surprised that this government took so long to react. We have had problems over the last year or so in Atlantic Canada. I am surprised that the government did not react quicker. I am disappointed that there is no plan in place for some of these other problems. I would urge the minister responsible, who happens to be from my home province, to get on with the job. We want action, less talk and more action.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a comment. I take quite well a couple of the suggestions which have been made by my friend, the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur, particularly as they involve the information systems and the gathering of information.
There is a recognition that while Dr. Harris has told us that we need more information, particularly information from the inshore-not that we do not from the offshore-it is important that the way we go about it is consistent with fishermen and the needs of fishermen. There is a program that is very effective in New Brunswick which involves the use of information gathered by fishermen, where the fishermen work with fisheries officers to put the information together. It is something that is an honour to participate in and it is something that has worked extremely well.
I think he knows as well as I that there cannot be an efficient program if the co-operation is not there. In my own province, where I think in the past it would be fair to say that there has not been the level of co-operation that has been essential, we are beginning to see that now with fishermen and scientists getting together.
With regard to the lack of resources, I think my friend knows that one of the criticisms of the $584 million Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program as the response to the crisis that we face, is that there is too much money
October 12, 1990

in there for bureaucrats and not enough for programming.
It is like the rock and the hard place. On the one hand we get criticized because we are not putting enough programming in place and, on the other, because we do not have the resources to enforce the laws and the regulations. We are trying to find the balance between the scientists and the enforcement officers. We need money going into programming so that we can develop other species with, test new gear and that sort of thing, but an important point has been made.
As for not being tough enough on Americans, I think my friend recognizes that it is an easier place to run away to than perhaps Portugal or Spain. I think it is fair to say that we have made great progress with colleagues of my friend opposite in reducing the European overfishing which started in 1972. In the last year we have seen less overfishing than we have seen perhaps in the last eight or nine years. I think there is progress because there has been a multi-faceted approach or a multi-targeted approach in dealing with some of the problems.
One will find that more of the efforts are going offshore in terms of implementation and enforcing regulations as we move to more observers, as we change the observers' status, as we do more gear testing, as we collect more information, and as we get more co-operation between the scientists and the large companies.
My hon. friend has a weakness that we all have; he freely admitted that he diverged a bit. I think it important that we put a couple of facts on the floor of this House.
Since 1977 the governments have moved a variable entrance requirement bill year by year. In 1989 this government, in recognition of the critical importance of the variable entrance requirement, instituted variable entrance requirements as part of the law. It did not need temporary implementation every year. It was institutionalized in the law. The majority of the members of this House and I voted for that legislation in November of last year. It has been sitting down the hall since then. In 1981, when the government opposite changed the regulations on unemployment insurance by moving from
Government Orders
eight to ten weeks, it did not get stuck down there two seconds.
I do not want to hear any more piety from my friends across the way about variable entrance requirements or anything else. They should tell the people in my constituency who want to get trained about the Senate and the variable entrance requirements. I voted for it and I expect the people down the way who are not elected or accountable to vote for it as well.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from St. John's East had a few comments to make. I would like to reply to some of them.
The bill that he is referring to, Bill C-21, has not become law. In the meantime, if he was thinking of the good of his constituents and the rest of Canadians, he would have asked his government to pass the variable entrance requirements. There are some problems with Bill C-21. Maybe the hon. member is becoming too partisan. When $2.7 billion is removed from the unemployment insurance fund by this government, who is it going to hurt? Employers and employees are going to have to pay the shot from here on in.
Let us talk about training. All the training in the world does not necessarily produce jobs. Where are the jobs? Training for what? It is fine and dandy to say there is training money there. We are not going to stoop to passing a bill just for the sake of getting some training money. There is no guarantee that that training money is going to be there long term. There is no guarantee that after that training money comes into place we are going to have jobs.
The unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces is in the high teens and in some places in the twenties. Training is not going to guarantee that there are jobs. They are cutting back regional development grants. They are cutting back CAP. They are cutting back left and right. That is all they do is cut, cut, cut, and the money that they get is transferred from one to another. They talk about an access centre for youth-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Have faith in the people.

speechtext:

October 12, 1990
