Mr. Speaker, for a while I thought we were debating Bill C-21, even though the issue is one that deals with fish and deals with an act to protect the fishing stock.
Oh, oh.

I hear the parliamentary secretary shouting from the other side. For a while I thought he might have some sort of difficulty breathing. Living in a democracy, however, I think it is only fair that when one member on one side of the House is speaking the other member on the other side of the House sits and listens. When he or she has a question, he or she will have the time to ask it.
First let me congratulate the parliamentary secretary as well as his minister on this wonderful initiative to move forward with legislation that will protect ultimately the fishing stock in Atlantic Canada. The people of Atlantic Canada can become the beneficiaries as a result of that.
Having said this, there are certain aspects of the bill that I think the parliamentary secretary as well as the minister responsible should take note of. One of them is the issue of enforcement. Any law that we put in place will not work unless it is properly enforced. Enforcement has to apply to those who are in big industry and those who are in small industry. It has to apply to the big, small and medium sized industry.
Unfortunately, as it is right now there is fear in the industry that the small fisherman might be fined and, if he has to pay a fine, that it might mean the end of that particular fisherman, whereas a big corporation that is fishing illegally or is intruding in the industry might be in a position to pay the bill and move on and do it again. That is one of the concerns of members of the community in Atlantic Canada vis-a-vis the present bill.
Another concern which I think is fairly important to take note of is the bookkeeping requirement. Unfortunately, according to Bill C-74, section 61(2) states that fishermen and processors may be required to keep records of the number, sex, size, weight, species, product form or other particulars of any fish caught. These requirements might put a tremendous amount of pressure on a small businessman or a small fisherman in the industry. I for one do not know whether a fish is a male or female. I do not know whether any of my colleagues on this side of the House would know how to identify a
female fish from a male fish. There are some who have indicated that they probably would know. This kind of requirement might put some pressure on the small businessman. It might increase the cost involved. Other concerns are the resources and personnel needed to enforce the present act, which I have already indicated, and that is yet to be seen.
More important than anything is the minister's own admission that the new act will be a part of the solution to many of the fishery's present problems. He then concedes that more must be done for the conservation of stocks. He clearly indicated that surveillance is a step in the right direction but that it is not the answer to all of the problems in the fishery today. I agree with the minister. I think it is a very sensible statement on his part. I think we have to do more for the fishing industry.
But I think what has to be done in Atlantic Canada is that the economy has to be diversified. We have to start providing alternatives to the fishermen, alternatives to the people of Atlantic Canada. The people of Atlantic Canada are not interested in handouts. The people of Atlantic Canada are interested in jobs, job creation and opportunities. They want to be considered as equals to the rest of Canada.
To that extent, my colleague from New Brunswick a little earlier made a statement about the need of infrastructure in Atlantic Canada. I want to reiterate that there is a definite need for infrastructure in Atlantic Canada. There is no point in talking about preserving the fishing stock because as you know, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing there that will stay forever. If the fishing stocks are not depleted today, tomorrow or the day after, they might be. What needs to be done is to provide alternatives.
Infrastructure is one of those options that is available to the government in order to move in and provide the services required. Then we will stop seeing raw sewage being dumped right in the ocean.
For instance, in Newfoundland there are 40,000 homes that do not even have proper pipelines for water, proper water, proper water treatment facilities and so on. Those are the kinds of things that the government can do today at a time when we are facing a difficult economic

October 12, 1990

situation. It can provide alternatives to the people of Atlantic Canada.
I am shifting away from the main topic a little bit but I just could not help it. I have visited many parts of Atlantic Canada. I came to the conclusion that the only way we can deal with the difficult economic situations in Atlantic Canada is through diversification of the economy, through proper job creation by providing the tools to the people so that they can deal with the issues effectively-
Those tools are the infrastructure. The infrastructre is missing there. Until such time as we deal with the heart of the problem, which is to provide them with the proper infrastructure required, they are going to be handicapped in the area of employment.
I want to conclude on a quick note by saying that those are the kinds of initiatives we would like to see taking place. I would like to commend my colleagues from Atlantic Canada who came in full force to speak in support of the bill. That is what it is all about. When something good is being done by the government, tell the government it is good and give them the credit for it. I was very happy to see my colleagues doing just that. There is much more that needs to be done. This is not the answer to an ongoing problem. This is the beginning of the solution.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to make two very quick comments. First of all, I am delighted to see my member of Parliament stand up and speak about the Atlantic fishery.
You're lucky to have such a good member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: You are very right.
You're lucky to have such a good constituent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
I am sorry La Pointe is not in his riding, but I am very pleased that our central Canadian members are prepared to stand and speak on this issue.
We all recognize that it is not an Atlantic issue. The fishery is a national issue. If we have been able to accomplish anything over the last couple of years in terms of overfishing or in terms of the crisis we face, is that we have allowed all Canadians to see this Atlantic
Government Orders
issue as a national issue. The fact that the member for Ottawa Centre and others stand and speak is important.
I want to comment very briefly on the question of tools. He is right when he talks about the Atlantic future being in the diversification of the economy, partly based on what we have now and what is there.
What Newfoundlanders want are opportunities. They are asking us to provide them with the opportunities and the tools. One of the most important tools we can provide to anyone in the world is an education, training and technical capability because without it there can be nothing. Without something to build on, there can be nothing. If there is anything that Bill C-21 does, it provides Atlantic Canadians with that tool. One of the most adventuresome projects that the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador share is one called the youth strategy. My friend from Burin-St. George's is familiar with it. One of the unusual things the government did was that it did not go into this program with preconceived notions. It had a mass consultation and talked to 600 groups that serve young people. It held consultations with young people across the province.
One of the things that came out of those six meetings, and I participated in one in Goose Bay, was that the young people said: "We know that you can't necessarily provide us with a job. It's not the job we want from you, it is the opportunity and the tools, because we will either find the job or we will create the job". Bill C-21 does exactly that. I thank my friend for mentioning that and giving me the opportunity to point out how important that piece of legislation is for the future of the Newfoundland economy and fishery.

Mr. Speaker, most of the hon. member's comments are well put, and I see my colleague from Newfoundland pointing across the floor. There is a lot of enthusiasm on both sides of the issue, but there is one point which I think is extremely important.
The parliamentary secretary has stated the need for education, especially in Atlantic Canada. Forty per cent of the youth do not finish high school.
That moves me to the second statement, that there is a need for an overhaul of the education system. I would like to enlist the support of the parliamentary secretary later this fall when I introduce a private members' bill in the House which will ask for a national standard for education so children in Newfoundland will have the same kind of education that children in British Columbia

Government Orders
receive. In that way we will have equality in education, so our school system will provide the tools for our youth, and older people who wish to go back to school.
There is no doubt in my mind that the only way we can deal with the issue of full employment is through a proper education system going back to the grass roots level, the source of the problem, and teach the youth from age five and provide them with the proper tools.
I am very happy to see many of my colleagues on all sides of the House speak a little more about the issue of education. I think it is important and timely, especially when we talk about 1990 being the international year of illiteracy. I know the minister of multiculturalism has done quite a bit in that field, and I am sure he will do more next week and the week after.
It is extremely important for us as a nation to be able to compete internationally. As we head into the 21st century, we must prepare our kids and provide them with the tools they need. We must prepare a proper national strategy that deals with education and provide a national standard for education.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for Ottawa Centre for taking an interest in a very valuable Canadian resource such as the fishery.
The variable entrance requirements have been passed in this House since 1977, and if they had been enacted people in Atlantic Canada would not have suffered as much as they have.
Shame, shame.

Whatever House it is in, people are suffering.
With this new bill, we will have fishermen keeping
books on the size, weight, sex of fish. All of that information will cause the fishermen a lot more problems.
Do you think they can tell them apart?
Good question.

Well, it is questionable if they can tell them apart or not.
We also have a problem in the fishery, as the government indicates, and it will crack down on the fishermen.
Are you going to hit them over the head with a hammer?

When the American scallop draggers come into our waters, we have a destroyer there. All that happens is that the scallop dragger rams our Canadian destroyer and runs back home. Is this what we call taking care of our resource? I would like to ask my hon. colleague if he believes there is enough enforcement in the fishery to take care of our waters and our valuable resource?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question. He comes from the wonderful island of Prince Edward Island. I do not know about the amount of fish that exists around the island.
One of the concerns I mentioned a little earlier was that the enforcement mechanism had to be put in place. We can talk about all the laws and all the rules we want, but unless we have a proper enforcement mechanism those laws will remain on the books. I totally agree that there is a need for a proper enforcement mechanism. The government should and I am sure will take note of that.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I congratulate my friend and colleague from Ottawa Centre for his depth of understanding of the fisheries issues which he so clearly demonstrated.
Also, on my own behalf and I believe on behalf of my good friend from St. John's East I want to express tongue in cheek a little horror at his earlier statement about the fact that there will be a national standard for education. Does this mean that we in Newfoundland are going to be delimited by the standards that they have in Ontario on this matter? Is that what he is saying?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: No, no. Does that mean we have to talk like them?
There are some things that Newfoundlanders will never accept, I say to him.
You are not going to let him get away with that.
I believe the Ontario caucus has awakened.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will accept the point of order from the hon. member for York South- Weston since it is Friday afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I am not quite certain whether you have been following what my good friend and colleague has been suggesting, but he has suggested in the last few moments that those members who represent Ontario ridings and who were educated in Ontario somehow are less intelligent than other members in this House, or their level of education might be suspect.
I would ask the hon. member to indicate clearly to Canadians generally that he in no way intended to insult and offend people educated in Ontario.
Could I speak to the point of order, sir?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not think it is a point of order, but I will allow the hon. member to finish his comment and question to the hon. member for Ottawa Centre.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York South-Weston misunderstood. I was not pointing to a problem. I was offering a solution, that is to adopt the Newfoundland standard as the national standard.
On the matter of variable entrance requirements which continues-
You are giving us a higher standard.

Is it not self-evident that it is a higher standard?
On the matter of variable entrance requirements which seems to be sneaking into every aspect of this debate, I have to say to my friend from St. John's East that he can say as often as he wants to: "I voted for." The record shows that he voted agin. In December 1989 there was an amendment in this House and he stood and voted against it. I sat here and watched him vote against the VER, I say to him eyeball to eyeball. In June 1990,1 say to him eyeball to eyeball, he voted against it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member should refer to the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre and not the other member. It was not his debate; it was the debate of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre.
It is Friday afternoon, but I would hope that hon. members would stick to the rules a little.

It is a challenge, Mr. Speaker, but we will try to be equal to it. I apologize. I should be speaking to the gentleman from Ottawa Centre, who is the member of Parliament for the gentleman from St. John's East.
I want to say to him that his constituent, who also sits in this Chamber, has been misrepresenting unwittingly, I say to him, a situation. He has been alleging that he, the constituent of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre, has been going around and saying that he voted for the VER. I can testify and I can get about 84 affidavits to back me up when I say that he actually voted twice against putting an end to the misery of thousands of people in my riding who would like to be able to draw their benefits after 10 weeks.
Finally, Sir, on this mini sentence, his constituent is equally right that we have finally achieved national recognition for an important national issue called the fishery. Only one thing remains, and I wonder if he agrees with this. The only attention we have yet to get is the attention of the Prime Minister on this national fisheries issue.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite encouraging. I might add I am also the member of Parliament for my colleagues from Newfoundland on this side of the House. As you know, Mr. Speaker, every member of the House actually works in my riding and at times I wonder whether I want some of those members to be working in my riding. Unfortunately, living in a democracy we have to hear all the opinions.
I want to congratulate the hon. member on his hard work on behalf of his constituents. I would also like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary on having a big heart and being able and willing to take the criticism and the question from the hon. member on this side.
I will not be in a position to answer the question, since it was not put to me per se. It was really put through me

Government Orders
to the hon. member on the other side of the House. I hope that at the next possible opportunity that hon. member will answer the question so we can straighten up the issue on both sides of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa Centre has the ability of being a very good speaker. One day, he will become the Speaker of the House of Commons-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
-the way he handled that question.
On that basis questions and comments are now terminated. Debate, the hon. member for York South-Weston.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that your boots will be very difficult to fill, given the immense amount of experience that you have in the House and your ability to be fair to all members on both sides of the House.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak to Bill C-74 and note that it is 13 or 14 minutes before two o'clock and unfortunately I will not be able to conclude my remarks today. I look forward to concluding them next time that the government calls Bill C-74.
You are probably wondering, Mr. Speaker, why a member of Parliament from Toronto is standing to speak to Bill C-74, which is entitled an act to amend the Fisheries Act and to amend the Criminal Code in consequence thereof. My constituents in the riding of York South-Weston who are watching this afternoon are probably asking themselves what does our member of Parliament know about fish and the fishery.
A lot.

Well, my friend from Burin-St. George's says a lot, but I would never ever know as much as he does about the fishery and the problems of Atlantic fishermen.
The western boundary of my riding is the Humber River and I know-
It's full of fish.
It's polluted.

It's polluted. It is polluted because of the actions of a previous Conservative government in the
province of Ontario and because of the neglect and incompetence of that particular government. I do not want to see the waters off the coast of our Atlantic provinces end up like the Humber River that bounds the riding of York South-Weston.
The parliamentary secretary did indicate, seriously speaking, that he was pleased that other members are standing to speak to this important piece of legislation because he believes, as I believe, the fishery is a national issue. All too often members in the House defer to members from Atlantic Canada or from British Columbia on issues involving the fishery. Whether they represent urban ridings or rural ridings, or ridings that have a significant number of fishermen as constituents, the time has come for all members to participate and involve themselves in what is happening in the Canadian fishery. It is a significant part of the economy of a number of provinces, the Atlantic provinces, British Columbia, and other provinces of course. The economies of other provinces are affected by the fishery.
The Liberal Party is in general support of this particular bill, Bill C-74. The former member for Beausejour, Fernand Robichaud, spoke on this bill on June 19, 1990. Mr. Robichaud has since vacated his seat-in order to permit Jean Chretien to have the opportunity to run, to be elected, and to represent the Liberal Party here in the House of Commons-but he gave an excellent speech. I certainly commend it to all members who are concerned about this particular issue and members who might want to read about the concerns of a former member who has worked extremely hard to deal with the problems associated with the fishery.
The government introduced this bill on June 6, 1990 and it was given first reading on that date. It is now October 12 and second reading is still not complete. One of the concerns expressed by Mr. Robichaud and others in the Liberal Party is in respect of the delay in processing this particular piece of legislation.
After we conclude second reading, this bill will be sent to a legislative committee which will consider the provisions in this piece of proposed legislation. The legislative committee will have the opportunity to call forward witnesses. It will have the opportunity to ask questions of the minister. It will have the opportunity to review this bill clause by clause to ensure that, in fact, it is a perfect
October 12, 1990

piece of legislation. The bill, in its present form, is imperfect in respect of some of its provisions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How so?
My friend and colleague, across the way, asks, how so. I simply ask him to be patient. I know that one of the boundaries of his riding is the Humber River-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I'm on the west bank.

-the west bank of the Humber River and also Lake Ontario, as I understand it. He, too, is much chagrined by the policies of the previous Conservative government in Ontario and how the policies affected the cleanliness of that particular body of water. I know the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore will be speaking to this bill when it is called again, presumably some time next week.
In any event to get back to Bill C-74, the legislative committee will have the opportunity to examine, very closely, this particular bill which we support in principle. I want to make it abundantly clear that the Liberal Party does, in fact, support Bill C-74 in principle. But we would like to see the bill improved.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for significantly stiffer fines and penalties for fisheries violations and damage to fish habitat under the Fisheries Act. The government states that such higher fines and penalties will bring the Fisheries Act in line with the deterrents contained in the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act and the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. The new proposed schedule of fines provide for significant penalties. There is no question about that. We are looking at summary conviction offences that could result in fines of up to $100,000 upon conviction and $500,000 for prosecutions that proceed by way of indictment. The prosecution would have the alternative, under this legislation, to proceed either by way of summary conviction or, the more serious route, by indictment. Presumably, when dealing with individuals, the prosecutors will proceed by way of summary conviction and when dealing with persistent offenders and when dealing with corporations that wilfully, consistently, and persistently breach the provisions of this act, the prosecutors will proceed by way of indictment. That could result, in certain cases, in fines of up to $500,000.
Government Orders
I would very much like to know whether the government considered minimum fines. There are no minimum fines provided for under Bill C-74. There are other offences in the Criminal Code of Canada and other federal legislation that provide for minimum penalties. If the government is serious in terms of the sanctions, and it appears to be serious given that, for example, for the obstruction of a fisheries officer there is the possibility of a maximum fine of $1 million if the prosecutors proceed by way of indictment.
Presumably the government is serious about the sanctions that appear here. These are the maximum penalties that the court can hand out. It can also hand out prison sentences. If the government is serious about telling Canadians and the foreign pirates who have been pirating our fish stocks that we are serious about this particular legislation, then the government will consider and implement minimum fines so that upon conviction, there will be a minimum fine.
Under the bill now, a discharge, whether it be an absolute discharge or a conditional discharge, could be the result of an infraction under the act. That is not acceptable. When we talk about some of the offences that could result under this act, whether it be general fisheries offences, obstruction of a fishery officer, or pollution of fish habitat, we want to ensure that the proper messages are sent out and that this law acts as a deterrent for those who pollute the fish habitat. The Government of Canada will not tolerate the deliberate pollution of the fish habitat. I would ask that the parliamentary secretary consult with his minister and consider minimum fines when this bill is sent to committee.
The Liberal Party has articulated a number of concerns that we have with respect to this bill. The parliamentary secretary is well aware of the four specific concerns that the Liberal opposition has articulated. I have but two minutes to briefly talk about those four points. I will expand on those four points when given the opportunity when the bill is brought forward again.
First, we are concerned about the present surveillance efforts that appear to be concentrated on the inshore sector. In effect, the inshore fishermen, Canadian fishermen, would be targeted under this legislation. We are concerned about those foreign fishermen, as I indicated earlier, who are pirating unlawfully and deliberately depleting our fish stocks.

October 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
The second I want to make is with respect to the fishermen's associations. We know that the industry has generally supported tougher legislation. The fishermen's associations were not consulted on the final form of this legislation. I hope the parliamentary secretary takes note. Of course, he will ensure that they are invited to make submissions at the legislative committee. The associations are concerned and agree that tougher penalties are necessary, but they are asking if the proposed legislation will accomplish what it is intended to do.
The third point is with respect to the lack of a comprehensive strategy to apprehend the foreign violators, particularly the American fishermen on the Canadian side of the Georges Bank.
The fourth concern is with respect to the record keeping requirements under Bill C-74. They are extremely onerous. Under section 61.2, fishermen and purchasers will be required to keep records of the number, sex, size, weight, species, product, form and other particulars of any fish caught. Can you imagine, every fish caught in every boat by every fishermen will have to be counted-

The House resumed from Monday, September 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Boyer that Bill C-258, an act respecting the establishment of the Centennial Flame Research Award to publicize the contributions to Canadian public life of persons with disabilities,
be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CENTENNIAL FLAME RESEARCH AWARD ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to have the opportunity to speak in support of the principle expressed in Bill C-258, an act to establish the Centennial Flame Research Award to publicize the contribution to Canadian public life of persons with disabilities.
As one of the few members, if not the only member of this House, who has had the opportunity to serve as a provincial minister of social services, I have had the opportunity to work with many disabled people in their organizations over a four-year period. Whatever gains were made by my department during those four years were made with the support and assistance of disabled persons, sometimes their very sharp assistance.
Prince Edward Island recognized the work of disabled persons by proclaiming last week, October 1 to 7, Canadian Paraplegic Association Week. The week was set aside to generate a greater awareness of the needs of disabled persons while reflecting upon their achievements. The association has made significant accomplishments in advocating on behalf of individuals with needs for better accessibility, counselling and other services.
As a former minister of social services, I have personal knowledge of the many difficulties that disabled people experience in their efforts to take part fully in the life of their community. I have met with them individually and in groups. What was most striking about that experience was the fact that no matter how great were the discouragements they had to face, they seldom appeared to get discouraged.
I am aware that for almost a decade the disabled people of Canada tried to get the attention of Parliament and were finally successful 10 years ago with the excellent barriers report of the parliamentary committee on the disabled.
The strength of this present proposal is that it once again brings before Parliament the continuing need of disabled persons for encouragement and support and permits this form of debate in the House. However, even as I support the principle of this bill, there are several issues that require more attention. I wish to call them to the attention of the House in case there may be an agreement on the need to amend the present bill.
October 12, 1990

The amount is only $1,000 per year. It would be unreasonable to expect it to do a whole lot for disabled persons in Canada. For this reason, we should not overload the project by asking for any form of report to Parliament on the issue cited. Any possible competition among disabled persons in organizations in Canada for a $1,000 award could make the cost of the selection process far greater than the eventual benefits. For that reason, I believe that we should eliminate the competitive process.
The bill proposes a stand-alone award and not a supplement for funds available elsewhere for a specific project.
However, I would think that the award could be a supplement to existing scholarships, most of which could stand enrichment. For example, I think that eligibility for the award could be restricted to graduating students from senior high school grades for disabled and who have made a significant contribution to public life during their school years. This contribution could be demonstrated through receiving a scholarship award for such contribution upon high school graduation.
The Disabled Persons Participation Program of the Secretary of State already provides substantial grants to organizations of the disabled which dwarf the small amount to be awarded from the Centennial Flame.
It is important that the House not trivialize issues of concern to disabled Canadians by an inappropriate gesture on our part, no matter how well intended.
I am pleased to endorse the principle that the Flame funds be used for further participation in public life of the disabled persons in Canada. But in recognition of the limited amount of money available, I would urge that the bill be referred to a legislative committee to receive suggestions on improvements.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CENTENNIAL FLAME RESEARCH AWARD ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, am pleased to rise' this afternoon to speak briefly on this particular bill. I wanted to point out to my colleagues that the member of Parliament for Hamilton Mountain, who would have liked to have been here to take part in these proceedings, at least observe what was being said, was away at a national aboriginal network conference on disabilities. Consequently, she is on her way back and unable to be here. The hon. member is sorry about that.
Private Members' Business
She did point out to me, however, some of the concerns that she had that I shall share briefly with the House. My colleague has already mentioned some of them, so I shall do so rapidly.
The first one, of course, is the whole notion of helping those who have some need for special assistance. This is one that we can endorse. It is an important principle and we have no difficulty at all supporting it totally and completely.
We are concerned, however, because the amounts are really quite small-we are talking about roughly $1,000-for what I am told are approximately 3.3 million disabled Canadians. That is perhaps a conservative figure in the sense that it does not include a number of other categories that might be involved. It is simply not a large amount.
What can we get done in terms of research, or what have you, for $1,000 today? Our great fear is that while the principle is a sound one and the intentions are very noble, the amounts of money may be communicating a contradictory message. So, I would ask that we consider that very seriously.
As well, there is a reference to an award being made to a person. We wonder whether or not that should not be expanded to groups of persons because, there again, it limits.
We ask whether or not the committee should be expanded to include the Speaker of the Senate because the fountain is on the precincts of Parliament. While I can understand that there may be some reluctance on the part of some hon. members to include anyone from the Senate nowadays, I would hope that we could keep those two issues separate and consider that as a real possibility.
I want to point out as well that the amount set is part of the bill. There is some concern there. What if the amount set is not met? What if it is lower or higher? Are there ways of circumventing that and responding to it appropriately?

Briefly, we support this bill in principle. There is no problem. It is an important gesture. However, we are afraid the gesture will be symbolic rather than concrete, and since this award will be limited to a maximum of about $1,000-it is said 3.3 million Canadians are in this group-we wonder whether this restriction will be criticized. Are we perhaps sending the wrong message?

October 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
As I said before, we also want to consider the option of giving the award to more than one person, so that a team would be able to apply for the award. We also think perhaps the Speaker of the Senate should also be included, since the site is part of Parliament. Finally, I have some questions, and I suppose the hon. member opposite will have some answers. When we are talking about dollars and cents, is there a problem when the amount is not sufficient, if we have less or more than the prescribed amount? Those are my comments, Mr. Speaker. I am willing to join my colleagues in working on this bill so that this proposal can be implemented.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CENTENNIAL FLAME RESEARCH AWARD ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for a brief moment to point out that Bill C-258 submitted to the House by the member of Parliament for Etobicoke- Lakeshore is very simple and straightforward. All it is suggesting and requiring is that the coins thrown into the Centennial Flame be concentrated into one point. It now goes to the Secretary of State and is spread out, gosh knows where, but to worthy organizations. The bill seeks to concentrate this to a very worthy cause whereby any disabled person could apply from year to year for the receipts of the coins tossed into the flame.
I resent a little the kind of criticism that seems to be directed at this bill. Maybe my friends from the opposite side are not reading the bill, or maybe they have a copy of the old bill. I would refer them to paragraph 6 which
says very clearly that funds for the awards shall consist of all money collected from the Centennial Flame on Parliament Hill in Ottawa during the fiscal year preceding the granting of the award. It is very simple, very straightforward.
To publicize this, a plaque could be put at the Centennial Flame there telling people who visit the Centennial Flame exactly where the money is going to go. The amounts collected have been anywhere from $750 to $3,500. It is very worth while. I think we should get on with it and make sure that it does happen.
